query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing melt-based additive manufacturing with micro-cold-spray solid-state deposition of AlCrFeNiSi powder will suppress melt-pool thermal gradients and solidification defects, yielding near-zero to compressive as-built residual stresses, improved or at least non-degraded strength–ductility and fatigue performance, and reduced processing complexity (minimal supports and no mandatory stress-relief heat treatment) for sub-millimeter-scale components, within a defined micro-cold-spray processing window.
generation.material_initial_state: Gas-atomized AlCrFeNiSi quinary alloy powder (nominally near-equiatomic Al–Cr–Fe–Ni with Si addition), spherical morphology, d50 ~ 8–12 µm (range 5–15 µm), oxygen content <0.2 wt%, as-received without prior heat treatment.
generation.intervention: Switch the build process from high-thermal-load melt-based AM (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) to micro-cold-spray additive manufacturing (solid-state kinetic consolidation) using the same AlCrFeNiSi powder.
generation.conditions: Micro-cold-spray parameters: N2 or He propellant gas at 2–3 MPa; gas temperature 200–400 °C (below alloy solidus, only to lower critical velocity); de Laval micro-nozzle exit diameter 0.3–0.6 mm; standoff 2–5 mm; traverse speed 5–20 mm/s; layer height 10–30 µm; substrate temperature ambient to 150 °C; substrate material AlCrFeNiSi or a ductile metallic base plate; build in inert atmosphere or dry air with dew point < −20 °C. Target miniature geometries: micro-cantilevers, pillars, and lattice struts with thickness/diameter 0.3–0.8 mm and lengths up to 10 mm. Test conditions: room temperature mechanical testing; residual stress by XRD sin2ψ and incremental hole-drilling; density by Archimedes and micro-XCT; microstructure by EBSD/TEM; micro-tensile or micro-bend for strength/ductility; high-cycle fatigue at R = 0.1, 20 Hz, stress amplitude ~0.35–0.45× as-built UTS.
generation.structural_mediator: Inter-particle adiabatic shear bonding and severe plastic deformation zones that create ultrafine/recovered grains and high dislocation density at interfaces, with suppressed solidification microsegregation and minimized coarse silicide/intermetallic networks; a net near-surface compressive residual stress field from high-velocity peening.
generation.mechanism: Because particles remain solid, the process avoids melt-pool thermal gradients and solidification shrinkage that generate tensile residual stress and hot cracking. High-velocity impacts induce localized adiabatic shear and plastic flow that disrupt surface oxides and form metallurgical bonds at particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces. The severe plastic deformation refines grains and increases dislocation density without promoting large-scale phase separation or coarsening of brittle silicides; the repeated peening establishes compressive residual stresses in the near-surface. Collectively, these effects reduce as-built tensile residual stresses, mitigate microsegregation-linked embrittlement, and simplify fixturing (reduced distortion and support needs).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to components printed from the same powder by a conventional high-thermal-load melt-based AM baseline: (a) As-built principal residual stresses are reduced substantially (direction: lower tensile; magnitude: typically ≥50% reduction versus LPBF baseline and net compressive near-surface is expected); (b) Porosity is at least comparable and can be ≤1–2 vol% after parameter optimization; (c) Microhardness and yield strength are not lower and are likely modestly higher (direction: equal to slightly increased, on the order of +0 to +30%) due to work hardening and grain refinement; (d) Ductility (elongation or micro-bend deflection at fracture) is not degraded and may improve (direction: equal or higher) owing to the absence of solidification cracks and coarse brittle phases; (e) High-cycle fatigue life at a fixed normalized stress amplitude improves (direction: longer life; order-of-magnitude expectation: ≥50% increase) due to compressive residual stresses and cleaner inter-particle interfaces; (f) Processing complexity is reduced (fewer or no thermal distortion-driven supports; no mandatory post-build stress-relief to meet the same residual-stress targets).
generation.baseline: Melt-based AM of AlCrFeNiSi powder via LPBF on a 100–200 °C build plate, 200–400 W laser, 20–40 µm layers, scan speeds 800–1200 mm/s, argon atmosphere, using standard support strategies. Typical issues include high thermal gradients, tensile residual stresses requiring stress-relief heat treatment, microsegregation and intermetallic/silicide networks, distortion, and hot-cracking risk in thin features.
generation.boundary: Feasible when: (1) Powder particle size d50 5–15 µm and surfaces not heavily oxidized; (2) Particle impact velocity above critical (estimated >600–700 m/s) achieved with 200–400 °C gas heating; (3) Features ≥0.3 mm thickness/diameter to accommodate nozzle footprint; (4) Substrate hardness/ductility adequate to avoid excessive erosion but allow interfacial bonding. Risk of inadequate deposition if the alloy is too brittle in the as-atomized state (e.g., excessive silicide content) or if particle size is too large (>20 µm) for micro-nozzles. Resolution below ~200–300 µm and internal enclosed channels are challenging without specialized tooling. Optional low-temperature annealing (≤600 °C) could tune work hardening, but the core hypothesis does not rely on post-anneal.
generation.uncertainty: No temporally eligible direct evidence is provided here for micro-cold-spray of AlCrFeNiSi specifically. Deposition of hard/brittle high-entropy alloys by solid-state spray can be difficult if critical velocity is very high; mild gas heating may or may not suffice for this composition. The magnitude of residual stress reduction and fatigue-life gains is expected but not quantified for this exact alloy/geometry. Surface finish and porosity may require parameter optimization. Miniature feature fidelity is limited by micro-nozzle dimensions and may constrain geometry.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce statistically comparable miniature specimens from the same AlCrFeNiSi powder by (i) LPBF (baseline) and (ii) micro-cold-spray under the stated conditions. Geometries: micro-cantilever beams (0.5 mm thick, 5 mm long) and straight micro-tensile dogbones (gauge 0.5×0.5×3 mm). No post-build heat treatment for either cohort. Characterize density (Archimedes and micro-XCT), residual stresses (XRD sin2ψ on surfaces; incremental hole-drilling for depth profiles), microstructure (SEM/EBSD/TEM for grain size, intermetallic/silicide distribution), hardness (Vickers HV0.05), tensile/micro-bend strength and ductility at room temperature, and high-cycle fatigue (R = 0.1, 20 Hz, stress amplitude = 0.40× each specimen’s as-built UTS).
measurements: As-built principal residual stress magnitude and sign at the surface (XRD sin2ψ) and depth profile (incremental hole drilling).
Volumetric porosity and defect size distribution (micro-XCT, 1–2 µm voxel).
Microhardness HV0.05 and nanoindentation modulus/hardness maps.
Tensile strength and elongation (micro-tensile) or equivalent micro-bend strength/deflection.
High-cycle fatigue life (cycles to failure at fixed normalized stress amplitude R = 0.1).
Microstructure: grain size distribution (EBSD), inter-particle bonding morphology, and presence/scale of silicides/intermetallics (TEM/EDS).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Reject the hypothesis if any of the following hold for the micro-cold-spray cohort relative to LPBF: (1) As-built principal residual stress magnitude is not reduced by at least 50% on average and is not net compressive at the surface; (2) UTS or yield strength is lower by >5% without a compensating increase in elongation (≥20% relative increase), i.e., strength–ductility is not at least maintained; (3) High-cycle fatigue life at the specified normalized stress is not higher by ≥50% on average; or (4) Porosity is >2 vol% or significantly worse than LPBF under optimized parameters.
